newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU parliament drops demand for television quotas.
newsitem.headline: EU parliament drops demand for television quotas.

text.p: The European Parliament abandoned on Tuesday its long-standing demands for stricter limits on the number of Hollywood programmes on European television, sidestepping a showdown with EU capitals.

A large majority of Euro-MPs wanted a binding rule requiring that 51 percent of Europe's TV screen time be devoted to European works but the idea failed to get enough votes to force EU governments to negotiate.

The vote brings to an end one of the EU's longest-running sagas, concerning the EU's 1989 television-without-frontiers directive, which deputies had hoped to revise to break Hollywood's domination of EU television screens.

"Very powerful interests have won today," British Socialist deputy Carole Tongue, a member of the parliament's Culture Committee, told Reuters, pointing to the United States's $6 billion trade surplus with the EU in the audiovisual sector.
"It is a major defeat for the European audiovisual industry."

Luciana Castellina, chairwoman of the Culture Committee and a leader in the fight for tougher limits on Hollywood, said the fact that EU governments could ignore the wishes of many more than half the EU assembly showed a power imbalance in the bloc.
The parliament had been fighting a losing battle with EU culture ministers, who had made clear in advance they had no intention of curbing the prime U.S. export industry.

On Tuesday, deputies from the mainly Christian-Democrat European People's Party accepted free trade arguments advanced by the European commercial television sector and swayed the vote in favour of Hollywood.
"The interests which are represented in this conflict are very heavy," a downcast Castellina told a news conference.
With the prospect of stricter quotas, Hollywood and the European commercial television industry set up high pressure lobbying bases in Brussels.
Former French Culture Minister Jack Lang, whose country led a lone fight against other EU countries for stricter controls on U.S. culture, said Hollywood could sleep safely after the vote.
"Washington can be reassured. Whether it comes to Zaire or culture the majority of Europeans lie down when America tells them to," he said in a statement.
The parliament stuck by two other key demands, which will now be hammered out with EU governments and the European Commission.

It will press in talks with EU governments for all new television sets to be equipped within a year with a so-called V-chip, which would allow parents to screen out violent programmes from their children.
A spokesman for the EU's Culture Commissioner Marcelino Oreja said the demand was unrealistic as the technology would not be available in time.
Parliament will also press for rules to ensure that terrestrial television viewers can watch major sports events like the soccer World Cup even if pay TV channels secure exclusive rights.
But the parliament decided not to demand tougher rules for advertising and teleshopping.
